clue.text: Show contempt for church when snubbing cardinal's char

indicators.note: To snub is to cut someone dead, and here the cutting is literal: the letter named next is dropped out of the word in front.

parts.note: To scorn something is to show contempt for it.
North is a cardinal point of the compass, and this is the letter that gets cut.
CH is the standard abbreviation for church, the one printed on maps.

explanation.walkthrough: The cardinal is a compass point, not a churchman in red — the surface stands him next to the church precisely so you read him the other way.
explanation.definitionFit: To char is to burn a surface brown or black, which is what a hot iron does to a shirt or the sun does to grass.

clue.text: Family goes on vacation to northern capital

parts.note: Your kin are your family, your blood relations.

indicators.note: A word sent on vacation has its insides emptied and its house left standing, so only the letters at each end stay behind.

parts.note: First and last letters of the word, all that survives the emptying.
The little word is taken at face value and joined on as it stands.
N is the map abbreviation for northern.

explanation.walkthrough: 'Goes on vacation' reads as one phrase about a holiday, and that is the join: the verb is fodder and the holiday is the instruction to hollow it out.
explanation.definitionFit: Kingston is the seat of government of Jamaica, so the plain noun names the answer by the category it belongs to.

clue.text: Spooner's apostle's train makes scheduled stop

indicators.note: Spooner's marks a phrase whose opening sounds are to be swapped, after the Reverend Spooner's famous slips

parts.note: a train is a retinue of followers, a court
the apostle is Paul, so apostle's is read as of Paul

explanation.surface: A saint's railway journey that calls at the timetabled station.
explanation.walkthrough: 'train' gives COURT and 'apostle's' gives OF PAUL, so COURT OF PAUL; 'Spooner's' swaps the C and P sounds to make PORT OF CALL. A train here is a retinue, not a railway one.
explanation.definitionFit: A port of call is a place where a ship or traveller stops briefly on a planned route.

clue.text: Abigail is prepared for eavesdroppers

indicators.note: An eavesdropper only ever hears a word, never sees it written, so the sound is what has to match.

parts.note: Something prepared has been made ready, and that word spoken is spelt a second way.

explanation.walkthrough: Abigail arrives with a capital letter and reads as somebody's name; it is a job, and the whole clue turns on demoting it.
explanation.definitionFit: An abigail is a lady's personal maid, named after a servant in a Jacobean play and now surviving mostly in crosswords.

clue.text: Recidivist regularly concealed gear under rugby player's top

indicators.note: Letters tucked away at even intervals — every second one — inside the word that follows.

parts.note: A back is one of the players behind the scrum, and the possessive 's' comes along for the ride.
The top of a jar or a saucepan is its lid.

indicators.note: A down entry is read top to bottom, so whatever is under something else lands later in the answer.

parts.note: Every other letter of the word, starting from the second.

explanation.walkthrough: 'Rugby player's top' sounds like a shirt, which is exactly the picture wanted: it is two separate pieces, a position on the pitch and a cover for a pot.
explanation.definitionFit: A recidivist keeps relapsing into crime, and a backslider is anyone who slips back into old bad habits — the same relapse in plainer words.

clue.text: Weed provided by fellow impresario

indicators.note: The two words after it supply the letters themselves, handing them over in order with nothing done to them.

parts.note: Four consecutive letters straddle the join, the end of one word running into the start of the next.

explanation.walkthrough: Nothing is rearranged, removed or sounded here: the surface offers a showbiz backer and a chum, and the letters simply lie across the gap between them.
explanation.definitionFit: A weed, in the playground sense, is a feeble specimen of a person rather than a garden plant, and that insult is what the answer means.

clue.text: Straight man discovered aboard ship

indicators.note: Read it as dis-covered: the covering letters at either end come off, leaving what was underneath.

parts.note: A liner is a large passenger ship.

indicators.note: Whatever is aboard a vessel is inside it, so the uncovered letter is placed within the ship.

parts.note: Take the cover off each end of the word and this middle letter is left standing.

explanation.walkthrough: 'Straight man' looks like one phrase, the comedian's partner, and prising the two words apart is the whole battle — only the second is fodder.
explanation.definitionFit: Something linear runs in a straight line rather than curving — the adjective a mathematician uses of a graph that never bends.

clue.text: Flapper admits boss shot shooter

indicators.note: To admit someone is to let them in, so the bird's letters open up and take the other piece inside.

parts.note: A bird that flaps — the black, cawing sort.

indicators.note: Shot silk has its colours thrown through one another, and the same scattering happens to these four letters.

parts.note: The letters of the word, thrown into a new order.

explanation.walkthrough: 'Flapper' wants to be a 1920s dancer in a fringed dress. Hear the bird instead and the rest of the clue opens up.
explanation.definitionFit: A crossbow shoots bolts down a grooved stock, so the loose noun names the weapon by the job it does.

clue.text: Sausage French fry with oil, salt and bay occasionally

parts.note: a French fry is a chip

indicators.note: occasionally means only now and then, so every other letter of the ingredient list is taken

parts.note: the three ingredients oil, salt, bay run together, with and only joining the list

explanation.surface: A recipe: fry a sausage French-style, with oil, salt and a bay leaf now and then.
explanation.walkthrough: 'occasionally' takes the first, third, fifth letters and so on of OILSALTBAY, giving OLATA; the 'and' only joins the list of ingredients.
explanation.definitionFit: A chipolata is a small thin pork sausage.

clue.text: Cooler setter essentially renounced drink

parts.note: The setter speaks as 'I' — the person who wrote the clue is in it.

indicators.note: To renounce is to give something up, so the letter singled out as the essential one is surrendered.

parts.note: The pressed-apple drink, five letters long.
A word's essential letter is the one at its very centre, and this sits at the centre of that drink.

explanation.walkthrough: 'Cooler' first reads as a noun — an icebox, or a prison cell — when it is the comparative adjective, which is what makes the ending of the answer fair.
explanation.definitionFit: Both are comparatives for a lower temperature, and both carry the same second sense of a frostier manner towards someone.

clue.text: Set straight communist about conflicts without borders

indicators.note: To go about something is to go round it, so one piece wraps itself outside the other.
A word's borders are the letters at its two edges, and without them only the middle survives.

parts.note: Red is the standing crossword word for a communist, after the colour of the flag.
Conflicts are FIGHTS, and losing the letters at either edge leaves this.

explanation.walkthrough: The politics is the misdirection: 'communist about conflicts' reads like a news headline while both words are quietly doing letter work.
explanation.definitionFit: To right a capsized boat, or an old injustice, is to set it straight again, and the past tense matches the definition's.

clue.text: Fish captain primarily shipped to East End

indicators.note: the first letter is shipped off to the far (east) end of the word, a cyclic move

parts.note: a skipper is the captain of a boat or team

explanation.surface: A sea captain sends his catch to market in London's East End.
explanation.walkthrough: SKIPPER (captain) has its opening S moved to the end, as 'primarily shipped to East End' instructs. The East End is the old working-class part of London, which makes the surface read as a trade route.
explanation.definitionFit: Kippers are herrings that have been split, salted and smoked, so they are a kind of fish.

clue.text: Third nun wrongly charged with a cowardly crime

indicators.note: Something done wrongly has not been done in the proper order, which is the licence to put these letters in another one.

parts.note: Eight letters of fodder, taken exactly as the clue prints them.
A ninth letter joins the pile before anything is rearranged.

explanation.walkthrough: The surface has a nun wrongly accused, so 'charged with' reads as an indictment; in the parse it is only the join between the letters and their definition.
explanation.definitionFit: Knocking someone down and driving off without stopping is the offence the phrase names, and the cowardice is in the fleeing.

clue.text: One who wangles tip from passenger in taxi? Animal!

indicators.note: The tip of a word is the letter at its far end, the point it finishes on.

parts.note: To fiddle something is to wangle it by a little quiet cheating.

indicators.note: Here 'in' is a placing instruction rather than scene-setting: the letter goes inside the word that follows.

parts.note: A taxi is a cab.
The letter this word finishes on.

explanation.walkthrough: 'Tip from passenger' reads as coins handed over at the end of a ride, which is the picture the setter is selling; in the parse a tip is one letter.
explanation.definitionFit: A fiddler crab is the small shore crab whose one huge claw looks like a fiddle being bowed, so the definition names its class.

clue.text: Doctor initially assists German dissecting aged script consultant

indicators.note: To dissect is to cut something open down the middle, and whatever does the cutting lodges inside.

parts.note: The everyday abbreviation, as on a brass plate.

indicators.note: Initially means at the start, so only the opening letter of the word beside it is taken.

parts.note: The letter this word begins with.
Aged cheese or aged wine is mature.
G is the standard dictionary abbreviation for German.

explanation.walkthrough: 'Doctor' is a favourite anagram signal and here it is nothing of the kind — it stands for its own two letters, and the German is a letter too, not a person.
explanation.definitionFit: A dramaturge is a theatre's in-house adviser on texts, working with writers on the shape and staging of a play.

clue.text: One might provide over-optimistic worldview?

definitions.meaning: The surface sense: someone looking through rose-tinted spectacles, which is an attitude and not an object.
The setter's sense: not a philosophy but a literal view out, through coloured glass set in a cathedral wall.

explanation.walkthrough: There is no separable wordplay here, just one joke told twice: a rose window is the wheel of stained glass above a cathedral door, and a rose tint is what makes any view too sunny.
explanation.definitionFit: The answer is the great circular panel of stained glass in a cathedral's west front, and tinted glass is the literal way to see life too cheerfully.

clue.text: Italian lady returning an unspoken acknowledgement

indicators.note: Something returning comes back the way it went, so the letters are read from the far end towards the near one — right to left in an across entry.

parts.note: The article is taken at face value, both letters of it.
A nod is how you agree without saying anything.

explanation.walkthrough: 'Returning' looks like part of the picture — a lady coming home — and it is the instruction instead. The acknowledgement is unspoken because it is a gesture.
explanation.definitionFit: Donna is the Italian courtesy title placed before a woman's first name, the feminine counterpart of don.

clue.text: Subdued party with Nollywood's top actors

parts.note: A do is a party — an office do, a birthday do.

indicators.note: The top of a written word is where it begins, so only its opening letter is wanted.

parts.note: W is the standard shorthand for with, as in 'w/ milk'.
The opening letter of the name given here.
The cast of a film is its actors.

explanation.walkthrough: Nollywood is Nigeria's film industry, the third of the -ollywoods after Hollywood and Bollywood; the clue wants nothing from it but the letter it starts with.
explanation.definitionFit: Someone downcast has low spirits and lowered eyes, which is the quiet, flattened mood the definition asks for.

clue.text: See 13
Suture holds in tendon

indicators.note: To hold something is to keep it within you, so the first word closes around what comes next.

parts.note: To suture a wound is to sew it up.
The little word is taken exactly as it stands and slotted into the gap.

explanation.walkthrough: The surface is entirely surgical, so no word sticks out as an instruction; the whole battle is hearing 'suture' as a verb.
explanation.definitionFit: A sinew is the tough cord tying muscle to bone, which is what a tendon is — the same fibre under an everyday name.

clue.text: Random drunk entering city where many disembarked

indicators.note: entering puts the jumbled letters inside the city's letters

parts.note: NY is short for New York, the city

indicators.note: drunk means the letters of random reel about into a new order

explanation.surface: A random drunk wanders into town, at the spot where crowds came ashore.
explanation.walkthrough: 'drunk' scrambles random and 'entering' puts it inside the New York abbreviation. The definition points to the D-Day landings of June 1944.
explanation.definitionFit: Normandy in northern France is where Allied troops landed from ships on D-Day in 1944.

clue.text: Pub brawl after Welsh emptied fish cart

indicators.note: In an across entry whatever comes after something sits to its right, so these two pieces land at the end.
Empty a word and its middle is gone, leaving only the letters standing at the two ends.

parts.note: First and last letters of the word, all that is left once it is emptied.
The long snake-like fish, a crossword regular.
A bar is a pub, or the counter you order at inside one.
A row, rhyming with cow, is a noisy quarrel.

explanation.walkthrough: 'Welsh emptied fish cart' is nonsense as English, which is the tell that the clue runs its pieces out of order: 'after' sends the pub and the brawl to the back.
explanation.definitionFit: A wheelbarrow is the hand-pushed garden cart with a single wheel at the front, so the definition names the class it sits in.

clue.text: Partially retired middleman enjoys dental cover

indicators.note: Only part of what follows is wanted — a run of letters sitting inside the words, not the words themselves.
Someone retired has withdrawn and gone back, and the letters go back too, read from their end towards their start.

parts.note: Six consecutive letters straddle the join between these two words, sitting there the wrong way round.

explanation.walkthrough: 'Partially retired middleman' is a plausible little biography and every word of it is an instruction — part of it only, and read backwards.
explanation.definitionFit: Enamel is the hard glassy layer capping a tooth, so the two words name it by where it lies and the job it does.

clue.text: See 13
Character in novella that you consider memorable, ultimately

indicators.note: What is ultimate comes last, so from each word you take the letter it finishes on.

parts.note: Three words in a row, each handing over the letter it ends on.
Three more final letters, still read left to right.

explanation.walkthrough: 'Character in novella' is the trap: it reads as somebody in a book, and the instruction sits right at the far end of the sentence, after a comma.
explanation.definitionFit: A person's nature is their character, the settled disposition you mean when you call someone good-natured.

clue.text: Tom consumes hot water in French stately home

indicators.note: What is consumed is swallowed whole, so the letter after it disappears inside the animal named before.

parts.note: A tom is a male cat; the capital letter is the disguise.
H is the letter on the hot tap, and the standard abbreviation.
Eau is French for water, as in eau de cologne.

explanation.walkthrough: The definition is only the last two words: 'French' has been borrowed by the wordplay for its water, which is what makes the clue feel a word short.
explanation.definitionFit: A château is a French country house or castle, the grand seat of a landed family — their equivalent of an English stately home.

clue.text: Nobleman almost loses case

indicators.note: the case of a word is its outside, so its first and last letters are removed

parts.note: nearly means almost

explanation.surface: An aristocrat nearly loses a court case.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Case' reads as a lawsuit, but here it is the word's outer letters: NEARLY ('almost') 'loses case', shedding its N and Y.
explanation.definitionFit: An earl is a British peer ranking below a marquess, so he is a nobleman.

clue.text: Ornament from Norway acquired by purist

indicators.note: Whatever acquires something takes it in and keeps it, so the longer word closes around the single letter.

parts.note: A pedant is a purist about small rules.
N is Norway's international vehicle code, the letter on the back of its cars.

explanation.walkthrough: A pedant would be the first to tell you the two words are spelled differently, which is the joke the setter is leaning on.
explanation.definitionFit: A pendant is the ornament that hangs from a chain round the neck; the name comes from the French for hanging.

clue.text: Long needle supplier

definitions.meaning: The verb, not the adjective: to long for someone is to ache for them.
The needles are the stiff evergreen leaves of a conifer, nothing to do with sewing.

explanation.walkthrough: 'Long needle' reads as one object, a big darning needle, and the split falls straight through the middle of it — one word to each definition.
explanation.definitionFit: To pine is to long for somebody, and a pine is the evergreen whose leaves are needles — two senses sharing only a spelling.

clue.text: Thin bedcover Romeo brought in for model

indicators.note: one letter is brought in to take the place of another, a substitution

parts.note: a sheet is a cover for a bed
the Model T was Ford's famous car, so model gives T
R is Romeo in the NATO phonetic alphabet

explanation.surface: A flimsy bedspread is brought in to stand in for a model in a photoshoot.
explanation.walkthrough: In SHEET ('bedcover'), the R of 'Romeo' is 'brought in for' the T, which 'model' gives from Ford's Model T.
explanation.definitionFit: Sheer fabric is so fine it is see-through, so sheer describes something thin.

clue.text: Grown-up desperate to secure extremely destructive explosive

indicators.note: to secure means to hold fast, so the rearranged letters hold the other piece inside
desperate suggests wild disorder, so the letters of grown-up are rearranged
extremely picks the two outermost letters of destructive

parts.note: first and last letters of destructive

explanation.surface: A frantic adult clutching something very destructive and explosive.
explanation.walkthrough: 'desperate' rearranges grown-up into GUNPOWR, and 'to secure' has it hold DE, the 'extremely' letters of destructive.
explanation.definitionFit: Gunpowder is the original explosive, a mix of saltpetre, sulphur and charcoal.
